title: Kisa Gotami's song
hookLine: her own verses: good friends, grief, and the deathless found (Therigatha, Kisa Gotami)

lines: THE MUSTARD SEED: A COMMENTARY STORY.
cards: Friends come first. That's where Kisa Gotami's own song begins, before any grief.

The path met her before in the commentaries' story: the dead child carried from door to door, the mustard seed from a house where no one has died, every house with its dead. That story belongs to the commentaries.
In the Therigatha, in her own verses, she puts something else ahead of it.

teach.b: First, the opening. Good friendship, she says, has been praised by the Sage. Keep company with good friends, and even a fool would grow wise.
Stay close to good people; that's how wisdom grows, and in their company one is freed from every suffering. She puts this before anything else. Second, the grief.

teach.h: THE ROAD, THE PYRE, THE TEARS.
teach.b: Her verses do hold terrible loss: a woman on the road, giving birth far from home, a husband found dead, children gone, a family burned on one pyre.
The commentary connects these lines with Patacara; some readers hear them as Kisa Gotami's own. Either way, the song doesn't look away. It speaks of tears shed across countless lives.
Third, the turn. Bereaved, she says, looked down on, I reached the deathless. I have walked the noble eightfold path.
I have seen nibbana. I have looked into the mirror of the teaching. The arrow is cut out, the burden is set down.
Fourth, the shape: friends first, then grief, then freedom.
Read in that order, the friends aren't decoration. Even in the mustard-seed story she isn't alone: she knocks on door after door, and every household tells her the truth, someone has died here too.
The suttas have a word for this, good friendship, and when Ananda calls it half of the holy life, the Buddha corrects him: it's the whole of it. Kisa Gotami's song seems to agree.

how: Some Theravada teachers tell Kisa Gotami's mustard-seed story when they speak about death and grief, and return to good friendship when they speak of walking the path with others.

o: a teacher who must be obeyed
a good friend on the path
a relative by birth or marriage

games.q: Kisa Gotami's song and story: tap the pairs.
p: cut out, the burden set down
she says she has looked into it
called good friendship half the holy life

s: the mustard-seed story is told in Kisa Gotami's own verses
it's told in the commentaries. her verses in the Therigatha begin with good friends.
her song opens with praise for good friends
keep company with good friends, she says, and even a fool would grow wise.
it holds a woman's terrible losses and tears shed across countless lives, before it turns to the deathless.

games.q: you're Kisa Gotami, about to sing your own song, after the grief and after the freedom. what do you put first?
games.why: her verses open with good friendship, praised by the Sage: keep company with good friends, and even a fool would grow wise. grief comes after, then the deathless.

practice: Bring to mind a friend who stayed when things were hard, or told you a true thing kindly, and remember one moment with them: what they said, where you were, what the light was like. Then simply wish them well.
If you pray, hold them in your prayer; if you don't, hold them in your attention, the way you'd keep a hand on a friend's shoulder.

wordCard.voice: Kalyanamitta. A good friend, a friend in the good: friends first in Kisa Gotami's song, then grief, then the deathless found. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kalyanamitta: a good friend, a friend in the good. Kisa Gotami's song opens with good friendship.

carryVoice: Your line: good friends. Friends first, then grief, then freedom, in that order. Day seven hundred ninety, done.

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary on verse 114, and the Therigatha commentary (the mustard seed)
